title: How a recruiting firm should write an about page
metaTitle: How a recruiting firm writes an about page
excerpt: Name who runs the search and what they will refuse. An origin story stays only if it changes the decision to brief the work.
alt: A white geometric building with a glass wing and a cantilevered upper volume, an exterior that says institution before it says who does the work.
caption: The building is not the person who will be on the week-three call. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What belongs in the first line of a recruiter's bio?
faqs.answer: Name the kind of role they fill and the company shape, in words a hiring manager uses on a requisition. Follow with the verbs of the search: scorecard, research, debrief. A line about passion or connecting people does not tell the buyer who will handle a thin shortlist.

faqs.question: When should a recruiting firm keep its founding story?
faqs.answer: Keep a short origin paragraph only when it predicts how a search will be run, such as a refusal to start without a scorecard. A coffee-shop founding year does not change the decision to brief you. If you delete the story and the bios still hold, the story was atmosphere.

faqs.question: What should the about page ask the visitor to do?
faqs.answer: Ask them to brief a search with the people who run that work. If you assign a lead only after the brief, say so in a sentence you can keep. Keep candidate sign-up as a quiet text link so it does not compete with the brief.

sources.title: Influencing your title links in search results

markdown:
A recruiting firm about page is proof that specific people stand behind the search. Name who does the work, and why a hiring manager who has been burned before should care. Skip the origin myth unless it changes their decision to brief the search. Google's helpful-content guidance treats "who" as part of trust: it should be evident who is responsible, and a byline should lead to real background where a reader would expect one. An about page that never names a person fails that test.

The buyer is not choosing a legend. They are choosing who will be on the call in week three, when the shortlist is thin and the scorecard is under pressure. Write for that week.

## Name the person who will do the work

Start with the people who run searches, not with a group photo and a founding year. For each person, use four facts.

Their name. The kind of role they actually fill. What they do on a search, in verbs: write the scorecard, run the research, sit in the debrief. What they do not do. A researcher should not be introduced as a talent partner if they will not be the person the hiring manager calls when a finalist withdraws.

Keep the bios short enough to compare. A hiring manager with one open seat wants to see two or three relevant people, not a directory of the whole office. If the firm is one person, say so. A single clear bio is better than a team page of stock silhouettes.

Put the role family in the first line of the bio. "Runs retained searches for plant leadership in owner-operated manufacturers." A burned buyer can match that line to their requisition in a second. "Passionate about connecting people" matches every firm that has already wasted their quarter.

If a person is leaving, or only supports searches, do not present them as a lead. The about page is a promise of presence. Update it when the roster changes. An outdated name is a small lie, and this buyer is calibrated to small lies.

## Why this buyer should care

The second sentence is the reason, and the reason is the search, not the personality. "She has hired night-shift supervisors and will not stretch a scorecard to fill a slate" is a reason. "He loves the outdoors and lives with two dogs" is a life. The life can sit at the end of a bio if you want the firm to sound human. It cannot be the reason to brief you.

Write the reason as a constraint the buyer recognizes. You stay on retained work and decline contingency piles. You will pause a search rather than present a weak shortlist. You have sat on the hiring side of this role, if that is true, and you say in which kind of company. Do not borrow a biography the person does not have. A fabricated operator's eye is worse than a plain description of a good researcher.

Google also asks whether the content shows first-hand experience. On this page, first-hand means the work they have done, described specifically enough to check. "Twenty years in the industry" is a duration. "Twelve retained plant-manager searches in the last four years, all with a written scorecard before outreach" is experience. Only write the second sentence if it is true. A round number you cannot define is the kind of claim this buyer has learned to ignore.

Skip awards unless the buyer would know the award and it changes the brief. A badge wall is how firms decorate an about page when the bios do not yet say the work.

## When an origin story earns its place

An origin story earns a paragraph when it changes the search the buyer is about to brief. The firm was started by someone who had been mishired into a plant role and now refuses searches without a scorecard. That sentence can stay, because it predicts behavior. The firm was started in a coffee shop after a leap of faith. That sentence can go. It does not change the brief.

Use this test. Delete the origin paragraph. Read the page to someone who hires. If they would still brief the search, the paragraph was not doing the job. If they are newly unsure who will run the work, you deleted the wrong paragraph. You deleted a bio, or you never wrote one.

Keep the story in the founder's voice only if they still do the work. A firm that has grown past the founder should not lead with the founder's leap. Lead with the people on current searches. The founder can have a bio in the same format as everyone else, with the same demand: kind of role, verbs, a true constraint.

If you want one sentence of history, attach it to a practice. "We have filled this seat since the firm started, and we still decline it when the scorecard is a wish list." History in service of a refusal is useful. History as atmosphere is how a handshake photograph sneaks back in as prose.

## What does not belong in the bio

Cut the lines that could be swapped onto another firm's site.

"Results-driven." "People person." "Trusted advisor." "Passionate about talent." A burned hiring manager has read these on the firm that sent them thirty resumes and called it a shortlist. The words are not false so much as empty. They do not predict week three.

Cut the client logo row from this page unless you can say what you did. A logo without a role is a borrowed reputation. If you can name the kind of search and the constraint, that belongs on a proof page, and the about page can point to it in a sentence. Do not make the about page a second, vaguer case-study wall.

Cut the hobbies if they push the work below the first screen on a phone. The first screen of this page should still answer who fills the role the homepage named. A dog and a marathon can wait. If they cannot wait, the page is being written for the team, not for the buyer.

Titles need the same honesty. Google's guidance on title links warns against vague labels such as "Profile" for a specific person, and against boilerplate that makes every page sound the same. "About" is a vague label. "Who runs a plant-leadership search" describes the page. Give each person a heading with their name and the role family, and make that heading visually the title of their block. Do not give "Our story" the same size as the name of the person who will take the brief.

## A page the researcher will still sign

The people on the page should be able to read their own block without wincing. Sit with the researcher or partner and read the constraint aloud. If they say they would not actually refuse that, take it out. An about page that overclaims becomes an argument with your own site in week three, when the buyer quotes you.

Agree on a revision rule. Bios change when the role family changes, not when someone wants a fresher adjective. A quarterly pass is enough if the work is stable. The day a lead leaves is not optional. The hiring manager who briefs you from a bio of a person who no longer works there will treat every later sentence as decoration.

Keep a private note of the sentences you refused to publish. That note is useful the next time a new joiner asks to sound more senior than the searches they run. The page is a roster of present work. Seniority that is not yet true can wait until the searches are true.

## How the page hands the buyer back to the search

The about page is not the place to re-explain the fee or to list every offer. It has one exit that matters: brief the search with a named person, or at least with the role family that person runs.

The action can say "Brief a search with this team." If you assign a lead only after the brief, say that. "You will hear from the person who will run the search, not from a coordinator who will hand you off." That sentence is worth more than a chat widget. If you cannot promise it, do not write it. Promise the routing you actually use.

A short line under the bios can say what the brief should contain. The role. The company shape. What failed last time. You are not asking them to attach a compensation philosophy. You are asking for enough to know whether this team should take the call.

Do not add a second exit of equal weight for candidates. "Join our network" can be a text link in the footer of the page. If it is a button beside the brief, you have split the page again. The about page is for the buyer who is deciding whether these people are safe to trust with a search.

## A read-aloud test for the bios

Read each bio without the name. Ask a colleague which person it is. If they cannot tell, the bio is still a template. Add the verb and the role family until the paragraph could only belong to that person.

Then read the whole page to someone who has been disappointed by a search firm. Ask who would be on the call in week three, and what that person would refuse. If either answer is fuzzy, the page is still an origin myth with headshots.

Keep the page short. People do not come here for a chronicle. They come to see if a human will stand behind the offer they already almost believe. When the bios can carry a real search, the next piece they need is the story of a decision, not another adjective. Read [how a proof page should show the constraint and the decision](/blog/proof-pages-for-a-recruiting-firm) before you paste logos under the bios and call it evidence.

When you want to see how a page can name the work before it names the mood, look at [selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). The pattern to borrow is specificity, not a layout.
